meta_title: zkCoins — Private Bitcoin via Shielded CSV
meta_description: zkCoins brings true privacy to Bitcoin via Shielded CSV: amounts, sender, receiver and history stay off-chain, proven with zero-knowledge. Every state-advancing step publishes only a ~64-byte nullifier to Bitcoin — about 16 vBytes marginal. No soft fork, self-custodial. Built on the paper by Jonas Nick, Liam Eagen and Robin Linus (ePrint 2025/068).
og_title: zkCoins — Private Bitcoin via Shielded CSV
og_description: True privacy for Bitcoin via Shielded CSV — coin data stays off-chain, with every state-advancing step publishing only a ~64-byte nullifier to Bitcoin. No soft fork, self-custodial.
og_image_alt: zkCoins — private payments on Bitcoin, secured with zero-knowledge
hero_lede: zkCoins brings true privacy to Bitcoin. Amounts, sender, receiver and history stay off-chain — proven with zero-knowledge, while every state-advancing step publishes only a ~64-byte nullifier to Bitcoin.
tx_public_foot: ~140 vBytes · fully public · one per payment
compare_cap: Coin data never touches the chain. Every state-advancing step — sending, receiving, minting — publishes one ~64-byte nullifier to Bitcoin: about 16 vBytes marginal, versus ~140 for a regular transfer, and constant no matter how many coins it moves.
quote_text: "Use the chain for what the chain is good for, which is an immutable ordering of commitments to prevent double-spending."
quote_cite: — Robin Linus, co-author of Shielded CSV
paper_title: Shielded CSV: Private and Efficient Client-Side Validation
paper_subtitle: A privacy-preserving variant of Client-Side Validation, settled directly on Bitcoin.
meta_authors_dd: Jonas Nick (Blockstream) · Liam Eagen (Alpen Labs) · Robin Linus (ZeroSync)
meta_predecessor_dd: zkCoins (Robin Linus, 2023) · builds on the ZeroSync prototype
paper_abstract: Client-Side Validation decouples transaction validation from Bitcoin consensus by moving it to the recipient. Shielded CSV improves on prior CSV designs by hiding the transaction history entirely: each transfer leaks only a 64-byte nullifier to the chain, with the rest verified client-side via succinct zero-knowledge proofs. The protocol is compatible with Bitcoin as-is — no soft fork, no hard fork — and targets roughly an order of magnitude more transactions per second than the base layer alone.
paper_note: zkCoins v1 builds directly on the paper's on-chain model: every state-advancing step publishes its ~64-byte nullifier directly to Bitcoin as a half-aggregated signature, so the chain itself guarantees every nullifier a verifier needs for its double-spend checks — no off-chain batch data and no data-availability assumption for the accumulator. About 16 vBytes marginal per step, on the order of ~100 state transitions per second.
changes_h2: Private transfers, a tiny nullifier on Bitcoin
changes_p: Coin data stays off-chain. Every state-advancing step publishes only a ~64-byte nullifier to Bitcoin, proven with zero-knowledge — so privacy and a small on-chain footprint win at once.
concept1_v: Coin data never touches the chain. Every state-advancing step — sending, receiving, minting — publishes one ~64-byte nullifier to Bitcoin, and nothing legible about amounts or parties.
concept2_v: Unlike RGB or Taproot Assets, history stays hidden under a zero-knowledge proof. Recipients verify validity without ever seeing the lineage.
concept3_v: No soft fork, no hard fork. CSV protocols use the chain only for ordering and double-spend prevention.
concept4_h: A fraction of a Bitcoin transfer
concept4_v: Each transfer costs about 16 vBytes on-chain — a fraction of a ~140-vByte Bitcoin transfer, roughly an order of magnitude smaller — constant no matter how many coins it moves.
how_h2: The chain orders, the recipient validates
how_p: Traditional blockchains ask every node to validate every transaction. Shielded CSV inverts that — validation moves to the recipient, and Bitcoin does only what it is uniquely good at.
step1_d: The sender creates a transfer and generates a succinct validity proof of the coin's entire history — a constant size, no matter how old the coin is.
step2_d: The proof travels directly to the receiver, off-chain. Only sender and receiver — and whichever node they deliberately trust with the plaintext — ever see the amounts, parties and history; none of it is written to the chain.
step3_t: The nullifier is published to Bitcoin
step3_d: Every state-advancing step publishes its ~64-byte nullifier to Bitcoin as a half-aggregated signature — sending, receiving and minting alike. Publishing is permissionless and contention-free: any wallet can self-publish, and the chain itself holds every nullifier a verifier needs.
step4_d: The receiver re-verifies the coin's full zero-knowledge proof locally — a single constant-time check, no matter how long the coin's history — and credits it once the nullifier that created it is settled on Bitcoin at the standard depth of six confirmations.
step5_d: Bitcoin records each nullifier in canonical order, and the first on-chain occurrence of a transition's account state key selects its one valid transition. The chain's one job: guarantee each state is advanced exactly once — with no off-chain data required.
perf_row3_zk: Full against the chain observer — only the per-block transition count is public
boundaries_p: Privacy here is structural, not a bolt-on. It is worth being precise about what this protocol deliberately is not.
not1_p: It uses Bitcoin L1 directly — no separate consensus, no bridge to a foreign chain.
not2_p: No sequencer, no data-availability layer — the nullifiers live on Bitcoin itself. Validity proofs move peer-to-peer between sender and receiver; each transfer's ~64-byte nullifier anchors to Bitcoin L1.
not3_p: Privacy is structural, not obfuscation — a global anonymity set of every coin, not a small per-round pool.
not4_p: No native protocol token to bootstrap. Value lives in client-side-validated coins.
not5_p: It works on Bitcoin as it exists today — no consensus change, no new opcodes.
zkbtc_h2: zkBTC — Bitcoin in the shielded pool
zkbtc_p: zkCoins has no native protocol token. zkBTC is a different thing: a published token standard for locking real Bitcoin and holding it as a private, freely transferable coin that any holder can redeem back into on-chain BTC — without a central party's permission.
zkbtc_status_text: No implementation code exists yet, the design is not externally audited and not production-ready. zkBTC is a worked-out draft that names its own open questions — the specification lists fourteen of them, including one bound on the redeem side that is not yet mechanized.
zkbtc_c1_v: zkBTC is token standard 3 on the zkCoins protocol. No second protocol, no separate chain, no consensus of its own.
zkbtc_c2_v: Any holder may send zkBTC to any address — without the gatekeeper's permission, without its signature, without it being online.
zkbtc_c3_v: The reserve rests on BitVM2 — no federation multisig. Exit needs one registered operator that is live, liquid and willing, in an epoch that still has vault capacity.
zkbtc_c4_v: An optional gatekeeper screens the source of new deposits at mint time — and has no role at peg-out.
phase01_lede: The proving stack and the wallet–server boundary. Everything downstream depends on this.
phase01_i1_why: Move the state-transition circuit onto a recursion-native proving system with a SNARK-friendly hash.
phase01_i2_why: Single-host Apple Silicon target — no GPU farms, no cloud proving service. The wallet holds only the private key.
phase01_i3_why: The wallet signs a fixed protocol constant and binds the node-computed ProofData digest into the signature nonce via sign-to-contract. No in-browser zero-knowledge.
phase01_i4_why: Create account, mint, send, receive — the full user loop runs on a public Bitcoin testnet.
phase02_lede: Close the protocol gaps between "works on signet" and "safe with real Bitcoin".
phase02_i1_why: Eliminate the residual link between sender, recipient and coin identifier.
phase02_i2_why: Rebuilt purely from Bitcoin; final at 6 confirmations, the Bitcoin-standard depth.
phase02_i3_why: Recipients verify a coin's age locally without trusting any third party.
phase02_i4_why: The full set of formal properties from the Shielded CSV paper, encoded as failing-witness tests.
phase03_lede: Mint and burn against native BTC without trusting the issuer. The biggest user-facing trust gap closes here.
phase03_i1_why: The bridge sits outside the protocol. A 1-of-n BitVM2 peg is the target; burn-not-theft holds only under 1-of-N setup honesty, an in-window honest challenger, and sound circuit/graph crypto.
phase03_i2_why: A succinct proof that a deposit landed at depth ≥ 6 in the canonical chain.
phase03_i3_why: Bridge our recursion-friendly proofs into a verifier that Bitcoin script can check.
phase03_i4_why: Launch is BitVM2 with permissionless per-epoch operator registration — no federation-multisig product path. Liveness still needs at least one live, liquid operator.
phase03_i5_why: Full peg-in / peg-out roundtrip including a deliberately malicious operator scenario.
phase04_lede: Move value between Lightning and zkCoins atomically — no provider trust, no custodial bridge.
phase04_i1_what: HTLC on the nullifier funding transaction.
phase04_i1_why: Atomicity lives on Bitcoin layer 1, not on the private coin layer. Standard primitives, no soft fork.
phase04_i2_why: Buy with Lightning sats and sell back to Lightning sats, both directions trustless.
phase04_i3_why: Anyone can run a swap provider; the protocol enforces honesty, not the operator.
phase04_i4_why: A swap provider learns the LN side, never the zkCoins-internal graph.
phase05_lede: Replace the bridge technologies of today with the bridge technologies of tomorrow — without changing the protocol.
phase05_i1_why: Port to a smaller field with a faster hash once the upstream stack stabilises. Algorithmic structure stays.
phase05_i2_why: Drop-in successors to BitVM2 (Glock, Mosaic) cut on-chain dispute cost by two orders of magnitude. Circuit contract unchanged.
phase05_i3_why: Grow the operator set with independent parties until the 1-of-n honesty assumption is a meaningful one.
phase05_i4_why: A 30–60 contributor ceremony replaces the single-contributor Groth16 parameter set used to test the bridge verifier — zkCoins' own proofs are transparent (FRI) and need no setup.
roadmap_note: Note. Dates indicate target windows for the engineering work, not a guaranteed mainnet date. zkCoins runs in a public test environment until pre-mainnet hardening completes; no real Bitcoin is at risk before then.
investors_title: Direct channel for funds and angels
investors_intro: zkCoins brings Shielded CSV to a self-custodial wallet — private Bitcoin on L1, no soft fork. We keep an open line for venture funds, family offices and strategic angels evaluating the project.
investors_body: The protocol is built on published research (ePrint 2025/068), the stack is open source, and the roadmap is public. We are not actively raising — but we are open to conversations ahead of mainnet.
faq_a1: zkCoins is a self-custodial wallet for Shielded CSV, a privacy protocol for Bitcoin. Amounts, sender, receiver and transaction history stay off-chain, proven with zero-knowledge and verified client-side. Every state-advancing step — sending, receiving, minting — publishes one ~64-byte nullifier to Bitcoin.
faq_q2: Is zkCoins a new token or altcoin?
faq_a2: No — zkCoins is not a separate blockchain, altcoin, or native protocol token. It is a client-side-validation layer anchored to Bitcoin L1; value lives in client-side-validated coins. Moving on-chain BTC in and out uses a bridge, which is on the roadmap.
faq_q3: Does zkCoins require a soft fork?
faq_a3: No. Shielded CSV works on Bitcoin as it exists today — no soft fork, no hard fork, no new opcodes. The chain is used only for ordering commitments and preventing double-spends.
faq_q4: How does zkCoins keep transactions private?
faq_a4: Each spend is proven with a zero-knowledge proof and shared off-chain. Coin data — amounts, parties and history — never touches Bitcoin; only a ~64-byte nullifier per state-advancing step is published to the chain. What an observer can see on-chain is how many transitions happened per block, nothing about them.
faq_a5: Yes. The seed and the spend key are generated and stored locally and never leave your device — no node ever gets spending authority. For proving you delegate a separate, non-spending operational bundle to a node; self-hosting it is the trustless path. There is no coordinator and no custodian; the one documented limit is the prover you pick yourself, which is why the specification says to self-host or vet it.
faq_a6: Shielded CSV (Client-Side Validation) is a privacy-preserving Bitcoin protocol from the paper by Jonas Nick, Liam Eagen and Robin Linus (ePrint 2025/068). zkCoins v1 builds directly on it: every state-advancing step publishes a ~64-byte nullifier to Bitcoin, everything else verified client-side.
faq_q7: Is the publisher role actually decentralized?
faq_a7: Publishing is permissionless and contention-free: any wallet can self-publish its own transitions to Bitcoin, so there is no ordering slot to win and no single sequential writer. In v1 publishing is sponsored — a publisher pays the Bitcoin fee for the inscription it broadcasts and is not reimbursed; the protocol defines no fee, no fee coin and no revenue. If no sponsor publishes, the sender pays its own inscription cost. A publisher never holds custody and can at most censor or delay a transition, never steal or forge coins. Full breakdown on the docs' Risks page.

faq_a8: On Bitcoin. Every state-advancing step publishes its ~64-byte nullifier directly to the chain as a half-aggregated signature, so Bitcoin itself guarantees the availability of every nullifier a verifier needs for its double-spend checks — no off-chain batch data and no separate data-availability layer for the accumulator. The coin data — amounts, parties and history — still stays off-chain, proven with zero-knowledge, and is never needed to reconstruct the public double-spend view.
faq_a9: zkBTC is designed as token standard 3 on the zkCoins protocol — a slot the protocol specification explicitly reserves for later standards, while standards 1 and 2 are the ones normatively defined today. It locks real Bitcoin and holds it as a private, freely transferable coin that any holder can redeem back into on-chain BTC without a central party's permission. It is a design specification — no implementation code, unaudited, not production-ready.

zkbtc_meta_title: zkBTC — Bitcoin-backed private coins on zkCoins
zkbtc_meta_description: zkBTC is token standard 3 on the zkCoins protocol: lock real Bitcoin, hold it as a private and freely transferable coin, and redeem it back into on-chain BTC without a central party's permission. zkbtc_og_title: zkBTC — Bitcoin-backed private coins on zkCoins
zkbtc_og_description: Lock real Bitcoin, hold it privately, redeem it without asking anyone. Reserve on BitVM2, open permissionless operator registration, optional gatekeeper at the entrance only.
zkbtc_standards_note: The third issuance standard the zkBTC specification proposes for the protocol: standard 1 mints without a cap, standard 2 with a fixed cap — standard 3 only against deposited Bitcoin.
zkbtc_h1_accent: no custodian, redeemable without anyone's permission
zkbtc_lede: zkBTC is a token on the zkCoins protocol: every coin is minted against an equal amount of real Bitcoin locked at that moment. The reserve sits in vaults that can only move along pre-signed BitVM2 fraud-proof paths — not with a custodian. Redeeming needs no one's permission; it needs one registered operator that is reachable, liquid and willing.
zkbtc_stat3_lab: ways to freeze a circulating coin
zkbtc_quote: "A purely peer-to-peer version of private electronic cash backed by bitcoin would allow payments to be sent without revealing amounts or the transaction graph and without a custodian."
zkbtc_paper_title: zkBTC: Private Electronic Cash Backed by Bitcoin
zkbtc_paper_subtitle: Built like Satoshi's Bitcoin paper — twelve sections, from what a transaction is to how the Bitcoin reserve holds.
zkbtc_paper_dd_length: 9 pages · Typst source in the repository
zkbtc_paper_dd_license: MIT — free to read, free to cite
zkbtc_paper_abstract: Digital signatures and zero-knowledge validity proofs solve part of the problem — but the benefit is gone as long as a trusted party still orders the transactions or holds the backing bitcoin. The paper proposes a system that uses Bitcoin as an ordering layer and nothing else: every state transition carries its own recursive validity proof, and the only thing that reaches the chain is a 64-byte nullifier. zkBTC is the one-for-one backed Bitcoin token on that protocol.
zkbtc_paper_note: Why it is worth reading: the paper derives the construction from first principles and states its assumptions in plain words instead of hiding them — 1-of-N setup honesty, at least one honest challenger acting inside the challenge window, sound circuit and graph cryptography. Anyone who wants to check whether the arithmetic holds will find everything needed to do so.
zkbtc_what_h2: Not a protocol token — an asset on the protocol
zkbtc_what_p: zkCoins deliberately has no native token. zkBTC is a different thing: a published standard for how real Bitcoin enters the shielded pool, changes hands privately inside it, and comes back out — verified by the same circuit and the same nullifier accumulator as every other zkCoins asset.
zkbtc_privacy_h2: Public at the edges, private in between
zkbtc_privacy_p: Entry and exit are ordinary Bitcoin events and therefore visible to everyone. Everything in between is not.
zkbtc_viz_in_d: BTC is locked. Amount and time are on the chain.
zkbtc_viz_pool_d: Any number of transfers — each leaves a 64-byte nullifier and nothing more.
zkbtc_viz_out_d: BTC flows back. Amount and time are on the chain.
zkbtc_viz_cap: The edges are public. Who locks bitcoin and who takes it back is traceable with amount and time — no design changes that. In between, each step leaves a 64-byte nullifier on the chain and nothing else: no amount, no parties, no lineage.
zkbtc_flow_p: Six steps. The marker on the right says whether the step lands readable on the chain or leaves nothing but a 64-byte nullifier — every state-advancing step publishes one.
zkbtc_s1_d: The depositor pays into a deposit address. Only once every operator of the epoch has pre-signed the spending paths does the BTC move into the vault — until then the depositor can reclaim it through the refund path.
zkbtc_s2_d: If the asset designates a gatekeeper, it checks the source of funds, its own view of the chain, and whether the epoch's operator set contains at least one independent honest signer, before releasing the mint. Without it no new zkBTC comes into existence — and it cannot reach the ones that already do.
zkbtc_s3_d: The coin appears in the pool, bound to exactly the recipient address committed beforehand. Redirecting it is ruled out.
zkbtc_s4_d: From here zkBTC is an ordinary zkCoins coin: pass it on as often as you like, without asking anyone and without anyone reading along.
zkbtc_s5_d: The holder burns the coin and names the highest fee they are willing to pay. The gatekeeper has no role here.
zkbtc_s6_d: A registered operator fronts the BTC and reclaims it from the vault. Who takes that on is decided by the market — the holder themselves, if they registered as an operator and posted a bond before the epoch.
zkbtc_roles_h2: Who is allowed to do what
zkbtc_roles_p: The load-bearing rows from the specification. The telling ones are those where nobody can act — and the one right below them, which is the difference between cannot and will not.
zkbtc_matrix_note: Cannot is not the same as will not. Nobody can block a redemption in the protocol — but the coin is burned first, and it stays unserved until some registered operator fronts the BTC within the holder's maximum fee. The specification names this case and files it under liveness, not theft. Two more conditions belong to the rows above: no operator can empty the vault as long as at least one honest challenger acts inside the challenge window and the circuit and graph cryptography is sound, and a holder can front a payout or register as an operator only after posting a bond before the epoch.
zkbtc_roles_caption: What each role can and cannot do under token standard 3
zkbtc_r2: See a depositor's off-protocol identity data
zkbtc_r5: Block a redemption in the protocol
zkbtc_r6: Redirect a mint to another address
zkbtc_r8: Front a payout and charge a fee
zkbtc_risks_p: The six points that a valuation runs into first. The specification lists twelve — this is not the whole list, and the whole list is worth reading.
zkbtc_risk1: Conditional guarantees, not unconditional ones. "No operator can steal" holds under 1-of-N setup honesty, at least one honest challenger acting inside the challenge window, and sound circuit and BitVM2-graph cryptography. A critical soundness bug enables actual theft.
zkbtc_risk2: Liveness, not custody. Exit needs at least one registered operator that is live, liquid and willing to front BTC. A redemption burns the coin first — a fee set too low leaves it unserved until someone takes it on.
zkbtc_risk3: The gatekeeper is a real trust concentration. In gated mode a compromised or negligent gatekeeper can enable a backing drain of the entire pooled reserve. And if it withholds its mint signature after the backing transaction has fired, the depositor's already-vaulted BTC becomes an irrevocable contribution to the reserve — a loss path on the depositor's side.
zkbtc_risk4: Pooled contagion. The reserve is pooled and the token is fungible — a single drained vault dilutes every holder, not just the counterparty of one deposit.
zkbtc_risk5: The edges are public. Amounts and timing at peg-in and peg-out are observable and correlatable, even though transfers inside the pool stay shielded.
zkbtc_risk6: Burned is burned. With no security council and no admin keys, the worst case under the trust model is a freeze or burn of the affected deposits — potentially permanent.
zkbtc_gates_p: The specification names two gate families that must both clear before an asset may be called zkBTC: four maturity gates, one of which is met, and four REQ-4 gates that carry the redemption guarantee itself.
zkbtc_g1_d: Bitlayer's BitVM bridge since July 2025, Citrea's Clementine since January 2026. The reserve construction is no longer research.
zkbtc_g2_d: Bonding, registration ceremony, and a policy that keeps any single party from dominating an epoch.
zkbtc_g3_d: The zkCoins predicate has to be brought into a form BitVM2 can verify at all.
zkbtc_g4_d: Circuit, BitVM2 graph and pre-signed graphs, published before mainnet. Exactly the class of fault that would otherwise enable real theft — and sound circuit and graph cryptography remains a standing assumption even after the audit.
zkbtc_gates_note: Seven of the eight are still open. Alongside the four maturity gates above stand four REQ-4 gates — anti-domination in the operator market, setup integrity of the pre-signing ceremony, documented holder-to-operator onboarding, and challenger economics. As long as one box is empty, zkBTC is a specification and not a product.
zkbtc_faq_a1: zkBTC is token standard 3 on the zkCoins protocol: lock real Bitcoin, hold it as a private and freely transferable coin, and redeem it back into on-chain BTC without a central party's permission. Today it is a design specification — no implementation code, unaudited, not production-ready.
zkbtc_faq_a2: No. The reserve sits in vaults that can only be spent along pre-signed BitVM2 fraud-proof paths; there is no key that lets anyone move it at will. What zkBTC does depend on is liveness — redeeming needs at least one registered operator that is live, liquid and willing. And in gated mode it depends on the gatekeeper doing its entry checks honestly: that is a backing-safety dependency, not merely a liveness one.
zkbtc_faq_q3: What can the gatekeeper actually do?
zkbtc_faq_a3: It can refuse or approve new mints at the entrance and see where a deposit came from. It cannot freeze coins, block a transfer, refuse a redemption, redirect a mint, or touch the vault. It has no role at peg-out at all. In gated mode it is still a real trust concentration: a compromised or negligent gatekeeper can enable a drain of the pooled reserve.
zkbtc_faq_a4: Transfers inside the shielded pool reveal no amounts, no parties and no lineage — on the chain each leaves nothing but a 64-byte nullifier. Peg-in and peg-out are ordinary Bitcoin events, so amounts and timing at the boundary are visible and can be correlated; and once an operator claims its reimbursement, that claim marker links the redemption to its payout. The specification says plainly that zkCoins with a bridge has less privacy than zkCoins without one.
zkbtc_faq_a5: No. Two gate families have to clear first. BitVM2 on mainnet is met; still open are the operator market, the conversion of the compliance predicate, an external audit of circuit and graph, and the four REQ-4 gates that carry the redemption guarantee. Until then zkBTC is a published design, not a product.
zkbtc_faq_a6: No. Each zkBTC is minted against an equal amount of real Bitcoin locked at that moment; it is not a separate currency and not a native protocol token. zkCoins deliberately has none. That the backing holds afterwards is a conditional property, not an unconditional invariant — the conditions are listed under residual risks.
